Finding the area enclosed by a spiral or a flower-petal curve is hard in x-y coordinates but elegant in polar form. The polar area formula sums up thin pie-slice sectors instead of rectangles — the right tool for curves that sweep around a center.

To find area in polar coordinates, you do not stack rectangles — you sum thin circular sectors (pie slices). Each tiny sector has area (1/2)r²dθ, which leads directly to the polar area integral.

The Polar Area Formula

Area in polar coordinates
The area swept by r = f(θ) from θ = α to θ = β is A = (1/2) ∫αβ r² dθ. Each thin sector contributes (1/2)r²dθ — the area of a slice of angle dθ.
🧠 ANALOGY

Cutting a pizza into ever-thinner slices: each slice is nearly a triangle with area (1/2)·radius²·angle. Add up all the slices as the angle sweeps around, and you have the total area. That is the polar area integral.

Polar coordinates locate points by distance and angle instead of by x and y. For anything with circular or rotational symmetry — spirals, flower-petal curves, planetary orbits, antenna patterns — polar coordinates make equations dramatically simpler.

In polar coordinates, a point is given by (r, θ): how far it is from the origin (r) and the angle θ from the positive x-axis. It is a different address system for the same plane.

Polar and Rectangular Conversion

Conversion formulas
From polar to rectangular: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. From rectangular to polar: r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x.
🧠 ANALOGY

Rectangular coordinates are like giving directions as "3 blocks east, 4 blocks north." Polar coordinates say "head out at this angle for this distance" — like a radar bearing. Same destination, more natural when things rotate around a center.

Figure 1. A point in polar coordinates: r is the straight-line distance from the origin, θ is the angle from the positive x-axis.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — convert polar to rectangular
Convert the polar point (4, π/3) to rectangular coordinates.
1
x = r cos θ = 4 cos(π/3) = 4·(1/2) = 2.
2
y = r sin θ = 4 sin(π/3) = 4·(√3/2) = 2√3.
Rectangular: (2, 2√3) ≈ (2, 3.46).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Not every curve passes the vertical-line test — a circle, a spiral, the path of a projectile loop back on themselves. Parametric equations describe such curves by letting a parameter t (often time) drive both x and y. This is the natural language for motion and for curves that are not functions.

In parametric form, x and y are each functions of a third variable t: x = f(t), y = g(t). As t advances, the point (x, y) traces a curve — often a path through time.

Parametric Curves

Parametric equations
A curve given by x = f(t), y = g(t) for t in some interval. The parameter t determines both coordinates; eliminating t (when possible) recovers a relation between x and y.
🧠 ANALOGY

Think of a GPS tracker on a moving car. At each moment t it records a position (x, y). The trail of dots is the parametric curve — and crucially, it carries direction and timing, not just shape. The same loop can be driven clockwise or counter-clockwise.

Example: x = cos t, y = sin t traces the unit circle as t goes from 0 to 2π (since cos²t + sin²t = 1).

Slope of a Parametric Curve

Parametric derivative
The slope is dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt) — divide the two rates. This works even where the curve is not a function of x.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — slope on a parametric curve
For x = t², y = t³, find dy/dx at t = 2.
1
Differentiate each with respect to t: dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 3t².
2
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 3t²/(2t) = (3/2)t.
3
At t = 2: (3/2)(2) = 3.
dy/dx = 3 at t = 2.

Parametric Arc Length

Arc length (parametric)
L = ∫ab √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt — the parametric version of arc length, summing tiny hypotenuses as t runs from a to b.
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. For x = t² , y = 2t, find dy/dx at t = 1. Show your work.
Show worked solution

dx/dt = 2t, dy/dt = 2. dy/dx = 2/(2t) = 1/t. At t = 1: 1/1 = 1.

dy/dx = 1
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. For x = 3t, y = t², find dy/dx as a function of t. Work below.
Show worked solution

dx/dt = 3, dy/dt = 2t. dy/dx = 2t/3.

dy/dx = 2t/3
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

The parametric slope is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) — a quotient of the two t-derivatives, not dy/dt times dx/dt and not their sum. A common slip is to forget the division.

Key Takeaways
  • Parametric equations x = f(t), y = g(t) trace curves that need not be functions of x.
  • Slope: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
  • Arc length: L = ∫√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt.
  • The parameter encodes direction and timing, not just the curve's shape.

Components: dx/dt and dy/dt are the component velocities of the parametric motion — the rates of change of position, not the positions or accelerations themselves.

x and y are both driven by time t; the arrows show the direction of travel. Slopes come from the chain rule — dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) — and the curve can loop or cross itself, which ordinary y = f(x) graphs never do.

Taylor series express any smooth function as an infinite polynomial built from its derivatives. This single idea powers numerical computation, physics approximations (small-angle, relativity), and much of applied math. It is one of the most far-reaching tools in all of calculus.

A Taylor series rebuilds a function from its value and all its derivatives at one point. Centered at 0, it gets the special name Maclaurin series.

The Taylor Series Formula

Taylor series
Near x = a, f(x) = Σn=0∞ [f(n)(a)/n!] (x − a)ⁿ = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + (f″(a)/2!)(x − a)² + …. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0.
🧠 ANALOGY

Building a Taylor series is like reconstructing a melody from its starting note plus its rate of change, its curvature, and so on. Each derivative adds one more layer of detail; with infinitely many layers you recover the exact tune (the function).

A power series is an "infinite polynomial" — and it lets us represent complicated functions (eˣ, sin x) as sums of simple powers. This is how calculators actually compute these functions, and the gateway to Taylor series. First we must know where such a series converges.

A power series is a series whose terms contain powers of x: Σcₙxⁿ. For some x-values it converges; for others it diverges. The set where it converges is an interval, and its half-width is the radius of convergence.

Power Series and Convergence

Power series
A series of the form Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ centered at a. It converges for x within a distance R of the center — the radius of convergence — giving an interval of convergence from a − R to a + R.
🧠 ANALOGY

A power series is like a radio signal centered at a: it comes through clearly only within a certain range R of the tower. Inside that radius the series converges; outside, it breaks up (diverges). The edges of the range need to be checked individually.

Finding the Radius with the Ratio Test

Apply the ratio test to |cₙ₊₁xⁿ⁺¹ / cₙxⁿ| and require the limit < 1. Solving for |x| gives the radius R.

Find the radius and interval of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n.

2
Limit as n → ∞: |x|·1 = |x|. Require |x| < 1 for convergence, so R = 1.
3
Check endpoints. At x = 1: Σ1/n (harmonic) diverges. At x = −1: Σ(−1)ⁿ/n (alternating harmonic) converges.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The ratio test is the workhorse for series with factorials or exponentials — and it is exactly the tool that finds the radius of convergence of a power series in the next chapter. It often succeeds where comparison is hard.

The ratio test examines how each term compares to the one before. If terms shrink fast enough (ratio less than 1), the series converges. It is especially powerful for factorials and powers.

The Ratio Test

Ratio test
Compute L = limn→∞ |aₙ₊₁ / aₙ|. Then: L < 1 → converges (absolutely); L > 1 → diverges; L = 1 → inconclusive (try another test).
🧠 ANALOGY

The ratio L is the "shrink factor" between consecutive terms. If each term is reliably less than the previous (L < 1) — like a geometric series with ratio less than 1 — the sum stays finite. If terms grow (L > 1), the sum explodes.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — a factorial series
Does Σ 2ⁿ/n! converge?
1
aₙ = 2ⁿ/n!, so aₙ₊₁ = 2n+1/(n+1)!.
2
Ratio: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = [2n+1/(n+1)!]·[n!/2ⁿ] = 2/(n+1).

A series is the sum of a sequence's terms: a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + …. To make sense of an infinite sum, look at the partial sums and ask whether they converge.

Series and Partial Sums

Convergence of a series
The partial sum Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. The series converges to S if the partial sums Sₙ → S as n → ∞. Otherwise it diverges.

Geometric Series

Geometric series
A series where each term is a constant ratio r times the previous: a + ar + ar² + ar³ + …. It converges if |r| < 1, to the sum S = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, it diverges.

Walk half the remaining distance to a wall, then half of what is left, then half again… You take infinitely many steps but travel a finite total distance — you reach the wall. That is a geometric series with r = 1/2 summing to a finite value, even with infinitely many terms.

2

A sequence is an infinite ordered list of numbers, and the central question is where its terms are headed. This is the foundation for infinite series (the rest of this chapter) and for understanding limits of discrete processes — interest compounding, iterative algorithms, population steps.

A sequence is just a list of numbers in order: a₁, a₂, a₃, …, with a rule for the nth term aₙ. The key question is whether the terms converge to some limit as n grows.

Convergence of a Sequence

Sequence limit
A sequence {aₙ} converges to L if aₙ approaches L as n → ∞, written limn→∞ aₙ = L. If no finite limit exists, the sequence diverges.
🧠 ANALOGY

A sequence is like a series of measurements taken at steps 1, 2, 3, … If the readings settle toward a steady value (a thermometer approaching room temperature), the sequence converges. If they keep growing or bouncing, it diverges.

When a force varies as an object moves — stretching a spring, lifting a hanging chain, pumping water from a tank — you cannot use simple "force times distance." Integration adds up the work over each tiny displacement. This is calculus directly powering physics and engineering.

Work is force times distance — but only when the force is constant. When the force changes with position, you integrate: add up F·dx over every tiny step.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Integrals of powers of sine, cosine, and tangent appear constantly in physics and engineering — Fourier analysis, signal processing, and wave problems are full of them. A few identity-based strategies handle them all.

Powers of trig functions do not integrate directly, but trig identities reshape them into forms that do. The strategy depends on whether the powers are odd or even.

Powers of Sine and Cosine

Odd-power strategy
If sine or cosine appears to an odd power, peel off one factor, convert the rest using sin²x + cos²x = 1, and substitute. The peeled factor becomes du.
Even-power strategy
If both powers are even, use the half-angle identities sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 to lower the powers.
🧠 ANALOGY

The Pythagorean identity sin²x + cos²x = 1 is a currency exchange: it lets you trade sines for cosines whenever it is convenient. The odd-power trick spends one factor to set up a clean substitution with the rest.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Substitution undoes the chain rule; integration by parts undoes the product rule. It is the go-to technique whenever an integrand is a product of two different kinds of functions — like x·eˣ or x·cos x — that no substitution can crack.

When you face an integral that is a product of two unrelated functions, integration by parts trades it for a (hopefully simpler) integral. The whole method is one formula and one good choice.

The Formula

Integration by parts
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. You split the integrand into a part to differentiate (u) and a part to integrate (dv); the formula swaps the original integral for one involving du and v.
🧠 ANALOGY

Integration by parts is a trade: you hand over the hard integral and receive a different one in return. The art is choosing u so that du is simpler than u — then the integral you get back is easier than the one you gave up.

Choosing u: the LIATE Order

Pick u as whichever type appears earliest in this list (it differentiates toward something simpler); the rest becomes dv:

LetterType
LLogarithmic (ln x)
IInverse trig (arctan x)
AAlgebraic (x, x²)
TTrigonometric (sin x, cos x)
EExponential (eˣ)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — algebraic times exponential
Find ∫ x eˣ dx.
1
LIATE: Algebraic (x) beats Exponential, so u = x and dv = eˣ dx.
2
Then du = dx and v = ∫eˣ dx = eˣ.
3
Apply uv − ∫v du: x·eˣ − ∫eˣ dx.
4
= x eˣ − eˣ + C.
∫ x eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C. (Check by differentiating with the product rule. ✓)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE — the logarithm trick
Find ∫ ln x dx.
1
There is only one function — but write it as ln x · 1. Let u = ln x, dv = 1 dx.
2
Then du = (1/x) dx and v = x.
3
Apply: x ln x − ∫ x·(1/x) dx = x ln x − ∫ 1 dx.
4
= x ln x − x + C.
∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C. (A classic — worth memorizing.)
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 1. Find ∫ x cos x dx. (Let u = x, dv = cos x dx.) Show your work.
Show worked solution

u = x → du = dx; dv = cos x dx → v = sin x. uv − ∫v du = x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x − (−cos x) + C = x sin x + cos x + C.

∫ = x sin x + cos x + C
✐ PRACTICE — you try it
Problem 2. Find ∫ x e2x dx. (Let u = x, dv = e2x dx, so v = (1/2)e2x.) Work below.
Show worked solution

u = x → du = dx; dv = e2xdx → v = (1/2)e2x. uv − ∫v du = (1/2)x e2x − ∫(1/2)e2x dx = (1/2)x e2x − (1/4)e2x + C.

∫ = (1/2)x e2x − (1/4)e2x + C
⚠ COMMON PITFALL

Choose u to get simpler, not more complex. For ∫x eˣ dx, picking u = eˣ would give du = eˣ dx and v = x²/2 — leaving a harder integral. LIATE keeps you out of that trap.

  • Integration by parts: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du — the reverse of the product rule.
  • Use LIATE to pick u (Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential).

  • The goal is an easier remaining integral — choose u so that du simplifies.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP

Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.

Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Techniques of Integration

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Integration by Parts

▸ Integration by parts ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du . You split the integrand into a part to differentiate (u) and a part to integrate (dv); the formula swaps the original integral for one involving du and v.

Trigonometric Integrals

▸ Odd-power strategy If sine or cosine appears to an odd power, peel off one factor, convert the rest using sin²x + cos²x = 1, and substitute. The peeled factor becomes du.

▸ Even-power strategy If both powers are even , use the half-angle identities sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 to lower the powers.

Trigonometric Substitution

The Three Forms — Each form matches a right triangle. √(a² − x²) is a leg when x and a are the other leg and hypotenuse — so setting x = a sin θ just names the angle. You are reading the…

Partial Fractions

▸ Partial fraction decomposition Write a proper rational function as a sum of fractions with simpler denominators. For distinct linear factors , each factor (x − r) gets its own term A/(x − r) with a constant to be found.

Improper Integrals

▸ Improper integral (infinite limit) ∫ a ∞ f(x) dx = lim t→∞ ∫ a t f(x) dx . If the limit is a finite number, the integral converges ; if it is infinite or does not exist, it diverges .

📋 Applications of Integration

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Volumes by Disks & Washers

▸ Disk method Revolving y = f(x) around the x-axis, each slice is a disk of radius R(x) = f(x) and area πR². The volume is V = ∫ a b π[f(x)]² dx .

▸ Washer method If the solid has a hole, each slice is a washer (a ring): V = ∫ a b π([R outer ]² − [R inner ]²) dx . Subtract the inner disk's area from the outer disk's area.

Volumes by Cylindrical Shells

▸ Shell method Revolving around the y-axis, each shell at position x has radius x and height f(x). Its volume is 2π·(radius)·(height)·(thickness). Total: V = ∫ a b 2π x · f(x) dx .

Arc Length & Surface Area

▸ Arc length The length of y = f(x) from a to b is L = ∫ a b √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx . Each tiny piece of curve is the hypotenuse of a triangle with legs dx and dy = f′(x)dx.

▸ Surface area Revolving y = f(x) around the x-axis generates a surface of area S = ∫ a b 2π f(x) √(1 + [f′(x)]²) dx — the arc-length element times the circumference 2πf(x) it sweeps.

Work & Physical Applications

▸ Work integral If a force F(x) acts along the x-direction from a to b, the work done is W = ∫ a b F(x) dx . Each tiny displacement dx requires work F(x)·dx; the integral sums them.

▸ Hooke's Law A spring resists with force F(x) = kx , proportional to the stretch x (k is the spring constant). The work to stretch from 0 to d is W = ∫ 0 d kx dx = (1/2)kd².

📋 Sequences & Series

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Sequences

▸ Sequence limit A sequence {aₙ} converges to L if aₙ approaches L as n → ∞, written lim n→∞ aₙ = L. If no finite limit exists, the sequence diverges .

Series & Geometric Series

▸ Convergence of a series The partial sum Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. The series converges to S if the partial sums Sₙ → S as n → ∞. Otherwise it diverges .

▸ Geometric series A series where each term is a constant ratio r times the previous: a + ar + ar² + ar³ + …. It converges if |r| < 1 , to the sum S = a/(1 − r) . If |r| ≥ 1, it diverges.

▸ Divergence test (nth-term test) If lim n→∞ aₙ ≠ 0, the series Σaₙ diverges . (Caution: if the limit is 0, the test is inconclusive — the series might still diverge.)

Integral & p-Series Tests

▸ Integral test If f is positive, continuous, and decreasing for x ≥ 1, then Σ n=1 ∞ f(n) and ∫ 1 ∞ f(x) dx both converge or both diverge . Evaluate the (easier) integral to decide the series.

▸ p-series A series of the form Σ 1/n p . It converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1 — derived directly from the integral test and the p-test for integrals.

Comparison Tests

▸ Direct comparison test For positive-term series: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ and Σbₙ converges , then Σaₙ converges (smaller than convergent). If aₙ ≥ bₙ ≥ 0 and Σbₙ diverges , then Σaₙ diverges (bigger than divergent).

▸ Limit comparison test If aₙ, bₙ > 0 and lim n→∞ (aₙ/bₙ) = L where 0 < L < ∞ , then Σaₙ and Σbₙ both converge or both diverge . Useful when the inequality for direct comparison is awkward.

Alternating Series & Absolute Convergence

▸ Alternating series test An alternating series Σ(−1)ⁿbₙ (with bₙ > 0) converges if two conditions hold: (1) the terms decrease, bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ, and (2) bₙ → 0. Both are required.

▸ Absolute vs conditional A series converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges. If Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, it converges conditionally . Absolute convergence is the stronger, more robust property.

Ratio & Root Tests

▸ Ratio test Compute L = lim n→∞ |aₙ₊₁ / aₙ|. Then: L < 1 → converges (absolutely); L > 1 → diverges; L = 1 → inconclusive (try another test).

▸ Root test Compute L = lim n→∞ n √|aₙ|. Same conclusion as the ratio test: L < 1 converges, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive. Best when aₙ is an nth power.

📋 Power Series

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Power Series & Radius of Convergence

▸ Power series A series of the form Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ centered at a. It converges for x within a distance R of the center — the radius of convergence — giving an interval of convergence from a − R to a + R.

Taylor & Maclaurin Series

▸ Taylor series Near x = a, f(x) = Σ n=0 ∞ [f (n) (a)/n!] (x − a)ⁿ = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) + (f″(a)/2!)(x − a)² + …. The Maclaurin series is the case a = 0.

Working with Taylor Series

Three Manipulations — Knowing the eˣ series is like owning a master template. Want eˣ²? Stamp x² into the template. Want the derivative? Adjust each piece. You reuse one known result many times over — one memorized series, substituted into, differentiated, or integrated term by term, replaces a dozen separate derivations.

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Parametric Equations & Calculus

▸ Parametric equations A curve given by x = f(t), y = g(t) for t in some interval. The parameter t determines both coordinates; eliminating t (when possible) recovers a relation between x and y.

▸ Parametric derivative The slope is dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt) — divide the two rates. This works even where the curve is not a function of x.

▸ Arc length (parametric) L = ∫ a b √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt — the parametric version of arc length, summing tiny hypotenuses as t runs from a to b.

▸ Conversion formulas From polar to rectangular: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ . From rectangular to polar: r = √(x² + y²) and tan θ = y/x.
